topics.name: Remote Control Impossible from Headless VPS
topics.preview: Remote Control Impossible from Headless VPS

messages.content: Is it possible for you to access my computer and take action like opening a website, clicking, and entering text even though you're installed on a VPS? Right now, i'm using the desktop app.

Good question — the short answer is **no, I can't control your local computer from the VPS**. Here's why:

## Where the agent actually runs

Hermes Agent runs on the **VPS** (this Linux server). The desktop app you're using is an Electron client — it connects to the VPS over the network and renders the chat UI. All my tools, terminal access, and `computer_use` capabilities operate on **this VPS**, not your local machine.

## What `computer_use` would control

If I were to use `computer_use`, it would drive the **VPS's desktop** — but your VPS is almost certainly headless (no monitor, no desktop environment). Let me verify:

As expected — no display server (`DISPLAY` is empty). This VPS is headless, so `computer_use` can't even drive a VPS desktop, let alone your local machine.

## How it all fits together

```
Your local machine (Windows)          VPS (this Linux server)
┌─────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────┐
│  Hermes Desktop App     │  ──WS──▶ │  Hermes Agent process    │
│  (Electron thin client) │          │  - terminal, files, web  │
│                          │          │  - computer_use (dead)   │
│  Your real desktop ←───  │          │  - all thinking happens  │
│  (browser, apps, files)  │          │    here                   │
└─────────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────────┘
```

The desktop app is just a chat window — it sends your messages to the VPS and displays my responses. The agent brain lives entirely on the VPS. There's no built-in bridge for the VPS-side agent to reach back through the Electron client and control your local Windows desktop.

## If you want me to interact with websites

I can browse the web **from the VPS** using the `browser_*` tools — those launch a headless Chromium here on the server. I can navigate, click, and type into web pages, and show you screenshots. That's the closest thing to "open a website and interact with it" — but it all happens on the VPS, not your local browser.

Want to try that? Or was there a specific task on your local machine you were hoping I could help with?
I think there are certain websites that wont allow you to use a headless chromium browser.

Yeah, you're right — headless Chromium gets detected and blocked by a lot of sites (Cloudflare, bot protection, login walls, etc.).

But there's actually a middle ground here. The Hermes desktop app has a **built-in browser** — an in-app Chromium that runs on *your* local machine, not the VPS. Let me check how that works:

Good instinct — and you're spot on. Let me lay out the full picture:

## The three tiers of "browser control"

| Method | Where it runs | Real browser? | Sites that block it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `browser_*` tools (agent-browser) | VPS, headless Chromium | ❌ Headless | Yes — Cloudflare, bot detection |
| `computer_use` + GUI browser | VPS desktop | ✅ Real | No — but VPS has no display |
| Your local browser | Your Windows machine | ✅ Real | No — but no bridge exists |

The `browser_*` tools are explicitly flagged in the skill as vulnerable to detection: *"Aggressive bot-detection may challenge it"* and social sites (LinkedIn, Meta) are called out as problematic.

## Is there a workaround?

Let me check if agent-browser is even installed and whether there's a cloud provider option:

Agent-browser is installed. But the fundamental problem remains: it's headless Chromium running on this VPS, and sophisticated sites will fingerprint and block it.

## What you can actually do

Here are the real options:

**1. For most web tasks** — the `browser_*` tools work fine. Documentation, public pages, most SaaS apps, APIs... no issues. It's specifically sites with aggressive bot protection (Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome, etc.) that cause trouble.

**2. For bot-protected sites** — you'd need a "real browser" path:
   - Run Hermes **locally** on your Windows machine instead of the VPS. Then `computer_use` could drive your actual desktop browser.
   - Or keep the VPS but handle those specific sites manually on your end.

**3. Cloud browser providers** — the skill mentions Browserbase as a `browser.cloud_provider` option, which uses real browsers on residential IPs. That might bypass detection better than a VPS IP + headless mode.

**4. The desktop app `/browser` command** — this might open a browser in the desktop app that the agent could drive, but I'm not sure if it works across the VPS-to-desktop gap the way you're set up.

What specific sites are you running into trouble with? That'll help me figure out which path makes sense.
are there any chrome extensions that work with Hermes like the Claude in Chrome extension?
Good news — yes, there is! Let me dig into the details:

Yes! There are **two** browser-related options for Hermes, and they serve different purposes:

---

## 1. Hermes Browser Extension (the "Claude in Chrome" equivalent)

**GitHub:** [abundantbeing/hermes-browser-extension](https://github.com/abundantbeing/hermes-browser-extension) — 1.1k stars, v0.2.0 alpha

This is exactly what you're describing. It's a Chrome/Edge side panel that connects to your Hermes runtime. Key points:

- **Connects to your VPS** — supports "Remote API" mode, so it can talk to your VPS's Hermes server
- **Sends browser context** — current tab URL, selected text, page content are sent to Hermes as context
- **Full Hermes access** — models, tools, skills, sessions, memory all available
- **Hermes Assist** — recognizes 31 writing surfaces (Gmail, LinkedIn, Twitter, etc.) and offers site-aware drafting
- **Nine themes**, light/dark mode, voice dictation
- **Keyboard shortcut:** `Alt+H`

**Install (load unpacked, not on Chrome Web Store yet):**
```bash
git clone https://github.com/abundantbeing/hermes-browser-extension.git
cd hermes-browser-extension
npm install
npm run build
# Then Chrome → chrome://extensions → Developer mode → Load unpacked → select dist/
```

**Important caveat:** In v0.2.0, the extension does **not** let Hermes control your browser (no clicking, typing, navigating). It's a chat side panel that reads page context. Specifically: *"No debugger, nativeMessaging, cookies, history, bookmarks, checkout, navigation, or autonomous browser-control permissions."*

---

## 2. `/browser connect` — Hermes drives a REAL browser via CDP

This is the official built-in feature that lets Hermes actually click, type, and navigate in a real Chrome/Brave/Edge window. BUT — it requires the browser to be on the **same machine as Hermes**. So with your VPS setup, this won't work unless you run Chrome on the VPS (which doesn't have a display).

If you ran Hermes **locally** on your Windows machine, you could do:
```
/browser connect
```
And Hermes would drive your actual browser — no headless detection issues.

---

## The bottom line

| What you want | Best option today |
|---|---|
| Chat with Hermes about the page you're on | **Browser Extension** — install on your local Chrome, connect to VPS |
| Hermes clicks/types in a real browser (not headless) | Run Hermes **locally** + `/browser connect`, OR use a **cloud browser** provider (Browserbase) with residential proxies |
| Hermes drives a browser that isn't blocked by bot detection | **Cloud provider** (Browserbase/Browser Use) with anti-detect profiles, OR run Hermes locally |

The browser extension is worth installing regardless — even without browser control, having Hermes in a side panel reading your page context is pretty useful. Want me to help you set that up?
there's gotta be some github repo that allows for this on VPS
Found it! Two approaches that do exactly what you want — let's dig in:

Here are the repos that do exactly this — bridge a VPS agent to a real browser:

---

## 1. `browser-use` — Remote Browser mode ⭐ (most relevant)

**Repo:** [browser-use/browser-use](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use)  
**Skill:** `remote-browser` — *"Controls a local browser from a sandboxed remote machine."*

It supports connecting to a remote CDP endpoint:

```bash
# On VPS — connect to your local browser via CDP URL
browser-use --cdp-url ws://YOUR_LOCAL_IP:9222/devtools/... open https://example.com
```

The tricky part is exposing your local Chrome's CDP port to the VPS. That's where **Tailscale** comes in (you already have it per your memory). You'd:

1. Start Chrome with debugging on your Windows machine:  
   `chrome.exe --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir=C:\hermes-chrome`
2. Tailscale exposes it: `tailscale serve 9222` or just connect via Tailscale IP
3. Browser-use on VPS connects to `ws://100.x.x.x:9222`

---

## 2. `chrome-devtools-mcp` — Official Google MCP Server

**Repo:** [ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp)

This is what the **Hermes docs themselves recommend** for remote browser control. It's an MCP server that runs next to Chrome and exposes browser control via the Model Context Protocol. Hermes natively supports MCP servers:

```bash
# On VPS, add the MCP server (pointing at your local machine via Tailscale)
hermes mcp add chrome-devtools --url http://100.x.x.x:9222
```

Same prerequisite: expose Chrome's CDP from your local machine to the VPS.

---

## 3. Hermes native `browser.cdpUrl` config

The Hermes docs mention you can set a remote CDP URL directly in config:

```yaml
# ~/.hermes/config.yaml on VPS
browser:
  cdpUrl: "ws://100.x.x.x:9222"  # Your local Chrome via Tailscale
```

Then Hermes's `browser_*` tools would drive your local Chrome directly — no headless detection issues because it's your real browser with your real cookies and sessions.

---

## The practical path for your setup

You already have Tailscale. The missing piece is just:

| Step | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Your Windows machine | Start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` |
| 2 | Your Windows machine | Install Tailscale (you likely already have it) |
| 3 | VPS | Point Hermes at `ws://<tailscale-ip>:9222` via `browser.cdpUrl` |

Then Hermes drives **your real Chrome, with your real sessions/logins** — from the VPS. No headless detection, no bot blocking.

Want me to walk through setting this up? The Chrome launch command is the main thing you'd need on your end.
is there a mobile app for hermes?

Short answer: **no official Hermes mobile app from Nous Research yet**, but there are a couple of options.

**What's actually available:**

1. **Official Hermes** ships native apps for **macOS, Windows, and Linux** (desktop) + a web dashboard, but **no iOS/Android app** in the main product. The repo I'm in confirms this — the only clients are the CLI, the TUI (`ui-tui`), the Electron desktop app, and the web dashboard. No Expo/React-Native/mobile code here.

2. **Feature request open** — there's an official GitHub issue ([#11911](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/11911)) requesting a native mobile app with voice calling. Still just a request, not in progress as far as I can tell.

3. **"Hermex" (third-party, iOS only)** — a community/third-party iOS app by LumaDock. Free on the App Store, MIT-licensed, code on GitHub. iOS-only for now.

4. **A recent PR (#52673)** "feat(mobile): add native mobile shell for Hermes Desktop" — adds a standalone mobile app (Expo-based, validated on iPhone with Android config included). It's recent (about a month ago); whether it's merged into your checkout depends on the version. It's a *shell* around the desktop backend, not a full native rewrite.

**Practical ways to use Hermes on a phone right now:**
- **Web dashboard** — `hermes dashboard` serves a browser UI; open its URL on your phone's browser. That's the easiest mobile path and what the project officially supports.
- **Messaging gateways** — Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, etc. are first-class platforms, so your phone's chat app is effectively a Hermes client.
- **Hermex / the Expo PR** if you want a dedicated app.

Hermes doesn't ship its own proprietary app-store app — it's a gateway bot that you reach **through** existing messaging/UI apps. Based on the actual platform adapters in this repo (27+ supported), here are the best mobile access paths, ranked by popularity and how well they work on a phone:

## 1. Messaging apps (the main mobile path)
You connect Hermes as a bot and chat with it from the app you already have. The most popular ones with first-class mobile apps:

| App | Adapter in repo | Mobile fit |
|-----|------|-----------|
| **Telegram** | `plugins/platforms/telegram` | ✅ Best all-round — clean bot API, rich mobile app, buttons, voice |
| **Discord** | `plugins/platforms/discord` | ✅ Great if you already use it; servers + DMs |
| **WhatsApp** | `whatsapp.py` / `whatsapp_cloud.py` | ✅ Cloud API or Baileys bridge |
| **Signal** | `plugins/platforms/signal` | ✅ Privacy-first |
| **Matrix** (Element app) | `plugins/platforms/matrix` | ✅ Decentralized, excellent mobile client |
| **Slack** | `plugins/platforms/slack` | ✅ If you live in Slack |
| **LINE** | `plugins/platforms/line` | ✅ Popular in Asia |
| **BlueBubbles** | `gateway/platforms/bluebubbles` | ✅ iMessage on iPhone |
| **WeChat/Weixin, Feishu/Lark, DingTalk, QQ, Teams, Google Chat, Mattermost, SMS, ntfy, SimpleX** | various | Region/work-specific |

For a private, low-friction setup (which fits what you've done before), **Telegram is the community default** — it has the cleanest bot setup, a native mobile app on every platform, and support for slash commands, buttons, and voice messages out of the box.

## 2. Web dashboard in a mobile browser
`hermes dashboard` serves a browser UI, and the repo even has `web/src/lib/pty-mobile-input.ts` — meaning the dashboard is built to accept input from a phone browser. Not an app, but bookmarks to your server's URL on your home screen give an app-like experience.

## 3. Third-party AI-chat apps via the API server
Hermes exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API endpoint** (`hermes ... api-server`). You can point any OpenAI-compatible mobile client at it — **Open WebUI, LobeChat, LibreChat, ChatBox** all have mobile apps and can use Hermes as the backend with its full toolset.

## 4. Run Hermes directly on Android (Termux)
There's a `getting-started/termux.md` guide — you can run the agent itself on an Android phone, no server needed.

## Which should you pick?
- **Easiest, most popular:** Telegram bot → chat from the Telegram app.
- **Most private / no cloud:** Matrix (Element) or Signal.
- **Want a ChatGPT-style UI on your phone:** connect ChatBox/LobeChat to the Hermes API server.
- **Already self-hosting:** bookmark the `hermes dashboard` URL on your phone.

Yes—there **are good UI options now**, but Hermes still feels more mature as a terminal/messaging agent than as a mobile-native product.

### Best current options

| Option | Best for | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| **Hermes Desktop** | Best full GUI experience | Native desktop, not mobile |
| **Hermes Web Dashboard** | Browser-based configuration, sessions, monitoring, and chat | Chat is essentially the TUI embedded in the browser; not the slickest phone UI |
| **Open WebUI + Hermes API Server** | Best polished web/mobile-browser chat | Separate app/container to deploy |
| **Telegram** | Best practical mobile experience | Looks like messaging, not a dedicated agent dashboard |
| **Discord/Slack/WhatsApp** | Mobile access through an existing app | Platform UX and integration limitations |

### My recommendation for your VPS setup

Since Hermes is running headless on your VPS:

1. **For everyday mobile use: Telegram**
   - Voice notes and transcription
   - File/image attachments
   - Scheduled results and notifications
   - Slash commands
   - Works naturally from anywhere

2. **For a polished browser UI: Open WebUI**
   - Hermes exposes an OpenAI-compatible API server.
   - Open WebUI provides accounts, conversation management, responsive mobile web UI, and installable-PWA-like behavior.
   - Hermes still retains its tools, memory, skills, terminal access, and web search behind that interface.

Does Hermes have any kind of smart router skill that will help me decide what LLM model to use instead of me having to manually change the models?

Short answer: **No, Hermes does not have a content-based smart model router** — but there are a few mechanisms that *look* like one. Here's the full picture:

---

## What Hermes Actually Does (and Doesn't Do)

### ❌ No content-based auto-selector
There is no feature that looks at your question and says "this is a coding task → use Sonnet" or "this is simple → use a cheap model." Despite what the setup wizard writes to your config, the `smart_model_routing.enabled` key in `config.yaml` **is a non-functional stub** — it's written but never read by any runtime code. Enabling it changes nothing.

### ✅ What *does* exist

| Mechanism | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Provider fallback chain** | When your active provider errors (quota, rate-limit, 401), Hermes cascades to the next provider. This *looks* like model-switching but it's purely error recovery. |
| **MOA (Mixture of Agents)** | Fans your prompt out to several reference models and aggregates results. Combines models — doesn't *select* one. |
| **`openrouter/pareto-code`** | A single alias that auto-routes to the cheapest model meeting a minimum coding-quality score. Coding only, narrow use case. |
| **Auxiliary routing** | Vision, web extraction, title generation, etc. are silently routed to a cheap aux model in the background. This never affects your main chat model. |

---

## What You *Can* Do Instead

Since there's no automatic picker, your realistic options are:

1. **Manually switch models** — Use the composer model pill in the desktop app → **Refresh Models**, or run `/model <model-id>` in a session.

2. **Set up MOA deliberately** — If you want multiple models to weigh in on a response, configure MOA explicitly via `hermes config`. It's not "best model selection" but it does give you a blended answer from several.

3. **Pin `openrouter/pareto-code` for coding tasks** — Narrow but genuinely automatic for that use case.

4. **Use per-task model overrides on cron jobs** — Each scheduled job can be pinned to a different model independently of your live chat.

---

## Want a Workaround?

If you describe what you're trying to accomplish (e.g., "I want cheap models for quick questions and smarter ones for complex tasks"), I can help you wire up a practical setup — whether that's a MOA config, a specific provider chain, or a cron-job structure. ## The Feature: Samsung's "My FanCam"

Launched July 2026 in One UI 9 on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8. Named after K-pop "fan cam" culture — those videos where a single idol is tracked throughout a performance.

### How it works end-to-end:

1. **Post-capture, not live** — You record normally (wide, everyone in frame), then edit later. Works on videos already in your gallery too, not just new ones.
2. **Open in Gallery → Galaxy AI icon → My FanCam** — Galaxy AI scans the video and detects every person in the scene. Touch targets appear as overlays on each detected person.
3. **Tap a person** — You select who you want to follow.
4. **Pick aspect ratio** — Choose from 1:1, 3:4, 9:16, 2:3, 3:5, 4:5, 5:7 (optimized for Instagram, TikTok, etc.).
5. **AI reframes** — Galaxy AI crops into the original footage and keeps your chosen subject centered frame-by-frame. Processing takes seconds (on-device Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU).
6. **Save copy** — You get a new video that looks like a dedicated camera operator followed that person the whole time.

### What's impressive:
- **Post-hoc tracking** — You don't need to track during filming. Shoot wide, decide the star later.
- **Processing speed** — Seconds, not minutes, for typical clips. On-device, no cloud.
- **Works on ANY video** in your gallery, not just newly shot ones.
- **Multi-subject detection** — It finds everyone, you just tap.

### Limitations (confirmed by hands-on reviews):
- **People only** — Reviewers tried it on dogs and it didn't work. The model is person-detection-only.
- **Quality loss from digital crop** — You're zooming into existing footage, so resolution takes a hit, especially when the subject is far away.
- **Needs a trackable subject** — Heavy occlusion or subjects moving out of frame break it.
- **Exclusive to Z Fold 8 / Flip 8** (for now).

## How We'd Build It

The good news: because this is **post-capture** (not real-time), we're not constrained by mobile NPU latency. We can use heavier models on a backend. Here's the pipeline:

### The Tech Stack

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   USER UPLOADS VIDEO                  │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. FRAME EXTRACTION  (FFmpeg / OpenCV)              │
│     Extract all frames at source FPS                 │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  2. PERSON DETECTION  (YOLOv8 / YOLOv11)             │
│     Detect every person in first frame               │
│     → Return bounding boxes + confidences             │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  3. USER SELECTS SUBJECT  (UI overlay)               │
│     Tap a bounding box to pick the person            │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  4. OBJECT TRACKING  (SAM 2 or ByteTrack/DeepSORT)   │
│     Track the selected person across ALL frames      │
│     SAM 2: pixel-perfect segmentation masks          │
│     ByteTrack: lightweight bounding-box tracking     │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  5. SMART CROP WINDOW  (Smoothing + easing)          │
│     Compute crop rect → center subject               │
│     Apply smoothing to avoid jitter                  │
│     Handle edge cases (subject leaves frame)         │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  6. RENDER OUTPUT  (FFmpeg)                          │
│     Crop each frame to target aspect ratio            │
│     Encode to H.264/H.265                            │
│     → Instagram/TikTok-ready clip                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key Model Choices

| Layer | Option A (Heavy/Accurate) | Option B (Light/Fast) |
|-------|--------------------------|----------------------|
| Detection | YOLOv8x / YOLOv11x | YOLOv8n / MediaPipe |
| Tracking | **SAM 2** (pixel-perfect masks) | ByteTrack + YOLO per-frame |
| Reframing | Spline-smoothed crop window | Linear interpolation |

**SAM 2** (Meta, open-source) is the killer piece here — it does exactly what we need: you give it a prompt on one frame (a click, box, or mask), and it propagates the segmentation mask through the entire video. It tracks the object even through occlusions and deformations. It's what makes this feel magical.

### App Architecture

I'd build it as:

- **Frontend**: React/Next.js PWA — upload video, see detected people overlaid on first frame, tap to select, choose aspect ratio, preview/download result. This could live on your VPS alongside hermes-stitch.
- **Backend**: Python (FastAPI) handling the pipeline — FFmpeg frame extraction, YOLO inference, SAM 2 tracking, crop-window math, FFmpeg rendering.
- **Processing**: GPU server for model inference (even a modest RTX 3060 handles this fine). Could be your planned home GPU box or a cloud GPU instance.
- **Queue**: For longer videos, a job queue (Redis + Celery / BullMQ) so the user gets progress updates.

### What Makes This Better Than Samsung's Version

1. **Track anything, not just people** — SAM 2 segments any object. Cars, pets, skateboards, whatever.
2. **No resolution penalty if you plan for it** — Shoot in 4K/8K, crop to 1080p, still sharp.
3. **Multi-platform** — Web app works everywhere, not just Samsung foldables.
4. **Smoother tracking** — We can apply easing curves and cinematic crop movements instead of hard lock-on.
5. **Batch processing** — Make fan cams for multiple people from one video in a single pass.

### The Hard Parts

- **SAM 2 is heavy** — ~200M parameters for the smallest variant. Needs a GPU. Per-frame inference on CPU is impractical for anything longer than a few seconds.
- **Edge cases** — Subject leaves frame, gets occluded, lighting changes, multiple similar-looking people cross paths. SAM 2 handles a lot of this but not perfectly.
- **Crop quality** — Digital zoom always loses quality. We could add AI upscaling (Real-ESRGAN) as a post-processing step.
- **Cost at scale** — GPU inference per minute of video isn't free. For an MVP, the home GPU server idea you mentioned would be perfect.

Yeah, you're spot on — Supervision is a much better fit here than SAM 2, and here's why.

## Supervision vs SAM 2 — Different Tools for Different Jobs

**Supervision + trackers package (ByteTrack/BoT-SORT/OC-SORT):**

This is **bounding-box-level multi-object tracking**. Here's what happens:

```
Frame 0: YOLO detects Person A, Person B, Person C
         ByteTrack assigns: tracker_id=1, tracker_id=2, tracker_id=3
  
Frame 1: YOLO detects Person A, Person B, Person C  
         ByteTrack matches via IoU + Kalman filter → same IDs persist
  
Frame 50: Person B walks behind a pole (occlusion)
          ByteTrack: marks as "Lost", keeps buffer for 30 frames
          
Frame 55: Person B re-emerges  
          ByteTrack: re-matches → same tracker_id=2
```

The killer feature for us: once the user taps a person in one frame, we just note their `tracker_id` and grab their bounding box from every frame. Then smooth the center points, compute a crop window, render. That's the entire pipeline.

**SAM 2** gives you pixel-perfect segmentation masks — the exact outline of the person. Great for rotoscoping or background replacement, but for our use case (cropping to a fixed aspect ratio box), bounding boxes are actually what we want. SAM 2 is also ~200M params needing a GPU; ByteTrack runs on CPU after YOLO detection.

## The Revised "Hard Parts" Assessment

With Supervision in the mix, here's what actually changes:

| Concern | Before (SAM 2) | After (Supervision + ByteTrack) |
|---------|---------------|--------------------------------|
| GPU requirement | Yes — heavy model | GPU only for YOLO inference (lightweight) |
| Speed per frame | Slow (segmentation) | Fast (box matching only) |
| Occlusion handling | SAM 2 internal | ByteTrack's lost-track buffer (configurable) |
| Pet/object tracking | Yes (SAM 2 segments anything) | Yes — just swap YOLO model to one trained on your target class |
| Complexity | High | Low — Supervision is designed for exactly this |

So the actual hard parts become:

1. **YOLO inference speed** — Still need a GPU for reasonable throughput. A 30-second video at 30fps is 900 frames. On CPU that's painful; on a modest GPU it's seconds.

2. **Crop window smoothing** — Raw bounding box centers are jittery. Need to apply smoothing (moving average, spline, or Kalman on the crop position) so the output video doesn't look shaky. This is pure math, not AI — totally solvable.

3. **Edge cases in tracking** — If the subject leaves frame for longer than the `lost_track_buffer` (default 30 frames = 1 second at 30fps), they get a new ID when they return. We'd need logic to handle re-identification or just accept the limitation.

4. **Resolution loss from digital crop** — Same as Samsung's problem. Could add AI upscaling (Real-ESRGAN) as optional post-processing.

None of these are dealbreakers. Supervision + YOLO + ByteTrack + FFmpeg is a proven, well-documented stack. There are dozens of tutorials showing exactly this pipeline — the novel part is just adding the "tap to select → auto-crop → aspect ratio export" UX layer on top.

Found it! Let me pull the rest of this thread.

Here's the full pricing strategy discussion, reconstructed chronologically. It kicked off right after the account creation bug was diagnosed:

---

## The Pricing Strategy Discussion — #all-archeforge, Today

### How it started
The bug discussion revealed that the free tier has been broken for weeks — new users got stuck in a loop after registering and couldn't chat. Nobody notified the team. That surfaced the question: **what are we even offering for free, and how do we convert?**

---

### The Debate: Credit Card Upfront vs. No-Card Free Tier

**Adrian** kicked it off:
> *"Question about the charge. Even if they select free, are we taking a card at signup?"*

**You (Reggie)** were firm:
> *"No. We do not capture credit card info. Standard practice NOT to collect card info for the free version."*

**Adrian** pushed back:
> *"I'm sorta feeling like capturing the card is standard business practice for recurring charges."*

**You** held: *"Not when it's the free version."*

**Adrian** proposed the model:
> *"$0 charge day 1, $19.99 after 30 days (or whenever)"*

**You** deferred to data: *"See what's best practice and we can change it. I don't think that's what ChatGPT does."*

**Adrian** conceded: *"I made an assumption here that was wrong. I would have pushed back on this for sure."*  
**Ben**: *"I agree with Adrian."*

---

### Ben's Pricing Vision (the centerpiece)

Ben came in hot with a multi-part proposal:

#### 1. The Trial Model
> *"30 Days. Everything Included. No feature restrictions. No 'Pro features locked.' Let them experience the whole product. Then on day 30: 'Your SoulPrint has grown over the past month. Continue where you left off for $19/month.'"*

#### 2. The Reframe: From Subscription → Asset
> *"You're no longer charging $19/month for AI. You're charging $19/month to maintain and grow a digital asset that becomes more valuable every day."*

#### 3. The Progress Dashboard (retention hook)
> *"Throughout the trial, show progress. Imagine a dashboard that says:*
> - *✓ 18 preferences*
> - *✓ 6 active projects*
> - *✓ 4 important relationships*
> - *✓ 147 remembered conversations*
> 
> *Every week that number grows. They're watching an asset accumulate. People don't cancel assets. They cancel subscriptions."*

#### 4. The SoulPrint Score (gamified retention)
> *"Not a gamification score. A completeness score.*
> ```
> SoulPrint Completeness
> ██████████░░░░░░░░
> 56%
> ```
> *Imagine onboarding: 'Your SoulPrint is 8% complete.' —> '63% complete.' —> '94% complete.' Now leaving feels like abandoning something they've invested in."*

#### 5. The Regulatory Warning
He also dropped research on FTC/state AG rules about auto-renewal, emphasizing clear disclosure and easy cancellation — *"no bullshit UX tricks."*

---

### Nick's Counter-Proposal
> *"I think we should do a $1 'age verification' charge — give them 14 days free for a dollar, auto-renew 14 days later at $19."*

**Adrian**: *"Yup."* ... *"I almost typed nope. But maybe."*

### Your Stance (Reggie)
> *"Keep it simple. Ben's idea works."*  
> *"Whatever you guys want."*

### Adrian's Closing
> *"That concept would solve so many problems and might make some lucky brand a household name."*

### Ben's Cool-Down
> *"That's a lot of ideas floating around now. Let's let Reggie relax and take them in to see what's feasible within limited time constraints."*

---

## My Thoughts

This is actually a great discussion. Here's my honest take:

### What's strong
- **The reframe from "AI subscription" → "digital asset" is genuinely clever.** It changes the psychology from "what am I paying for this month?" to "I'm maintaining something I've built." That's the same mechanic that makes people keep paying for storage lockers.
- **The progress dashboard is a proven retention tactic** — Duolingo streaks, GitHub contribution graph, Strava stats. People hate losing visible progress.
- **No credit card for free tier is the right call.** ChatGPT doesn't do it. Claude doesn't do it. It kills top-of-funnel and you don't have the brand trust to ask for it.
- **30-day full-feature trial** lets the product sell itself by actually working.

### What needs caution
- **You need the product to NOT be broken during the trial.** The bug you just fixed was killing conversions silently for weeks. If the trial experience has friction, no pricing strategy saves you.
- **$19/mo might be low** for "digital asset maintenance." If the value prop is truly "your AI self that gets smarter over time," premium AI tools charge $30-200/mo. But starting at $19 to build a base isn't wrong — you can always introduce tiers later.
- **Nick's $1 verification charge** solves a real problem (bot accounts, payment method verification) but adds friction. The data says every extra step in signup costs you 10-20% of users. Only do this if spam/fake accounts are a measurable problem.
- **The SoulPrint Score** is powerful but must not feel like a dark pattern. If the score is real (actual usage data) and genuinely useful, it's brilliant. If it's gamified fluff, people will see through it.

### What's missing
Nobody talked about:
- **Annual pricing** (discount for commitment = better retention, upfront cash)
- **What "free" actually includes** after the 30 days — is there a permanent free tier, or is it trial-or-nothing?
- **Team/family plans** — "4 important relationships" in the dashboard begs for a shared plan
- **How many of the 201 subscribers are paying vs. free** — you need this data before setting pricing

**Bottom line**: Ben's framing is the right direction. The team is aligned. Just make sure the product works first — pricing can't fix a broken onboarding.

Here's what I found — there are **several** GitHub repos that let Hermes Agent talk to Claude Code and Codex, all without API keys (they use the locally installed, already-authenticated CLIs):

---

## 🏆 Top Pick: **hermes-code-bridge** (⭐27, most active)

**[github.com/xuyang-liu16/hermes-code-bridge](https://github.com/xuyang-liu16/hermes-code-bridge)**

This is a **Hermes plugin + skill** — the cleanest integration. Install in seconds:

```bash
hermes plugins install https://github.com/xuyang-liu16/hermes-code-bridge --enable
```

Then use the `/code-bridge` slash command. It turns Hermes into a command center for **Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI** — all locally, no API keys needed because it drives the CLIs that are already authenticated on your machine.

Example workflow:
```
/code-bridge Use Codex to implement the fix, then ask Claude Code to review the diff. Report evidence, tests, and risks.
```

---

## 🌉 **hermes-acp-bridge** — WebSocket upgrade for persistent sessions

**[github.com/memoverflow/hermes-acp-bridge](https://github.com/memoverflow/hermes-acp-bridge)**

Upgrades Hermes's built-in ACP (Agent Client Protocol) to **WebSocket transport** so Claude Code and Codex sessions persist across multiple calls (instead of dying after each one). Pure Python stdlib — no dependencies. Includes a real-time dashboard at `localhost:18081`.

---

## 🔀 **a2a-bridge** — Multi-protocol, multi-agent hub (⭐9)

**[github.com/firstintent/a2a-bridge](https://github.com/firstintent/a2a-bridge)**

The most ambitious: a **star-topology daemon** that translates between A2A, ACP, and MCP Channels so Claude Code, Codex, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, Zed, and VS Code agents all talk to each other. One-time install, pick your agents, bidirectional delegation. TypeScript/Node.

---

## 📋 **Rainhoole/hermes-agent-acp-skill**

**[github.com/Rainhoole/hermes-agent-acp-skill](https://github.com/Rainhoole/hermes-agent-acp-skill)**

A pure Hermes skill for ACP-style multi-agent delegation between Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code. No plugin required — just a skill you install.

## 🔧 Hermes also has this **built-in**

Looking at the skills you already have loaded — **`claude-code`** and **`codex`** are already part of your skillset. They use Hermes's `terminal` tool with `pty=true` to drive the CLIs directly (print mode `-p` for one-shots, tmux for interactive sessions). This is the "no external repo needed" path — you can already do:

> "Use Claude Code to review the auth module" or "Use Codex to implement a dark mode toggle"

...right now, using the skills you have. The repos above just make it more structured (persistent sessions, dashboards, multi-agent orchestration in one command).

**My recommendation:** `hermes-code-bridge` is the most polished and actively maintained (updated today, ⭐27). One `hermes plugins install` and you're done. Want me to install it?
yes and then show me how to use it

Installed and ready. Here's your practical guide:

---

## ✅ Installed

- **Plugin:** `hermes-code-bridge` (enabled)
- **Claude Code:** v2.1.201 ✓
- **Codex CLI:** v0.145.0 ✓

---

## Three ways to use it

### 1. The `/code-bridge` slash command (simplest)

Just type `/code-bridge` followed by what you want. Hermes routes it to the right CLI:

```
/code-bridge Use Codex to review my latest git diff. Read-only. Focus on bugs, security risks, and missing tests.
```

```

```

```
/code-bridge Use Codex to implement the fix, then ask Claude Code to review the diff. Report evidence, tests, and risks.
```

### 2. Multi-agent pipeline (the "coffee break" workflow)

You can chain agents. Tell Hermes once, walk away, come back to results:

```
/code-bridge Use Codex to run the experiment, then ask Claude Code to review the result. When done, summarize the commands, changed files, test results, failures, and remaining risks.
```

### 3. Background dispatch for long tasks

For tasks that take a while, Hermes dispatches them in the background and monitors:

```
/code-bridge Use Codex to refactor the auth module to use JWT. Run the full test suite after. This is a long task - run it in the background and report when done.
```

## What each backend is best at

| Backend | Best for |
|---------|----------|
| **Codex** | Implementation, debugging, focused repo changes |
| **Claude Code** | Careful code review, refactoring plans, reasoning-heavy debugging |
| **Kimi Code** | Long-context codebase understanding, Chinese/English mixed |
| **OpenCode** | Local project navigation, terminal-first coding |
| **Gemini CLI** | Quick inspection, lightweight review |

## Key safety rules (automatic)

- **Session-first routing** — reuses existing sessions instead of starting fresh every time
- **Confirmation before edits** — if a task modifies files or pushes code, Hermes asks first
- **Evidence ladder** — doesn't trust agent self-reports; verifies `git diff`, test output, and artifacts
- **Honest reporting** — says "blocked" instead of inventing results
- **No API keys needed** — uses the locally installed, already-authenticated CLIs

i've tried multiple times and it looks like it gets stuck:

/code-bridge can you build this for me? https://github.com/dylan-buck/Hermes-iOS
Please load and follow the `hermes-code-bridge:hermes-code-bridge` skill for this request.

User request:
can you build this for me? https://github.com/dylan-buck/Hermes-iOS

Three issues at play here. Let me break them down and build what we can:

---

## Why `/code-bridge` gets stuck

**The iOS app (`HermesMobile.xcodeproj`) can't be built on Linux** — it requires Xcode on macOS. Codex/Claude Code hit the same wall, and the bridge properly blocks rather than faking results.

But the repo has **two other components we CAN build**: the **connector** (Python) and **relay** (Python). Let me build those now.

---

## Summary — here's what happened

### There were 3 problems with `/code-bridge` getting stuck:

1. **The skill wasn't registered** — the plugin installed but `hermes-code-bridge` didn't appear in the available skills list for this session (needs a gateway restart). The plugin files are on disk, but Hermes can't see them yet.

2. **"Build" is ambiguous** — the repo has 3 separate components, and "build this for me" doesn't tell Codex/Claude Code which one. They'd try to figure it out, fail on the iOS part (Xcode/macOS), and hang.

3. **iOS can't be built on Linux** — `HermesMobile.xcodeproj` requires Xcode on macOS. No CLI agent can work around that.

### What actually got built:

| Component | Status | Tests |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| **iOS app** (`HermesMobile.xcodeproj`) | ❌ Needs macOS + Xcode | N/A |
| **Connector** (`connector/`) | ✅ Built | 78/83 pass (94%) |
| **Relay** (`relay/`) | ✅ Built | 47/47 pass (100%) |
| **hermes-ios skill** | ✅ Installed at `~/.hermes/skills/hermes-ios/` | — |

### How to use what's built:

**Relay** (the server your phone talks to):
```bash
cd /tmp/hermes-ios-build/relay
source .venv/bin/activate
cp .env.example .env   # edit DATABASE_URL + INTERNAL_API_KEY
uvicorn app.main:app --reload   # starts on :8000
```

**Connector** (runs next to Hermes, bridges relay ↔ Hermes):
```bash
cd /tmp/hermes-ios-build/connector
source .venv/bin/activate
hermes-mobile setup --relay-url http://your-relay:8000/v1
```

**To actually use the iOS app**, you'd need to open `HermesMobile.xcodeproj` on a Mac with Xcode and build to a physical iPhone.

### To fix `/code-bridge` for future use:

Restart the Hermes gateway so the plugin skills register:
```bash
hermes gateway restart
```

Then `/code-bridge` will have the skill loaded and can properly dispatch to Codex/Claude Code for tasks they can actually handle. The skill was never the problem — it was trying to build an Xcode project on Linux.

Short answer: **no — the VPS vs. laptop distinction is exactly why Desktop app is the right choice, and it makes no difference to the auth flow.** Let me explain why, because it's a common point of confusion.

## What actually matters for OAuth here

The OAuth "application type" (Desktop vs Web) is **only about how the authorization code gets back to Hermes** — it does *not* care where the code runs. The flow is:

1. Hermes (on your VPS) generates an auth URL and gives it to **you**.
2. **You** open that URL in a browser **on your laptop** and approve.
3. Google redirects your laptop's browser to `http://localhost:1?code=...` — which fails to load (expected), so **you copy the URL from the address bar** and paste it back to me.
4. Hermes (on the VPS) exchanges that code for a token.

Notice: at no point does anything need to *connect* to your VPS from Google or from your browser. The "redirect" never actually completes a network connection — it just puts the code in your address bar for you to copy. That's why **Desktop app** (which uses a `localhost` loopback redirect) works perfectly even though Hermes is on a remote server.

## Why Desktop app is correct here (not Web)

| | Desktop app | Web application |
|---|---|---|
| Needs a publicly reachable server? | **No** | Yes (Google pings your redirect URI) |
| Needs you to fill JavaScript origins / redirect URIs? | **No** | Yes |
| Works with Hermes on a headless VPS? | **Yes** (code copied manually) | Awkward — Google would try to reach `localhost` *on your laptop*, not the VPS |

A "Web application" type is for when Google must actually call back a real, internet-facing URL (like `https://myapp.com/oauth/callback`). Your VPS isn't serving a public OAuth callback endpoint, so Web type would be the wrong fit and force you to configure URIs that don't correspond to anything real.

## So:
- **Create it as Desktop app.** VPS location is irrelevant — the manual "copy the code from the address bar" step is what bridges your laptop to the VPS, and Desktop app is built for exactly that.
- The skill is hardcoded for this: it uses `http://localhost:1` as the redirect and reads the code you paste. No server-side listener needed.

Use when the user asks to "post AI news to LinkedIn", "share the latest AI news on LinkedIn", a daily AI-news LinkedIn update, or anything similar.

Two halves:
1. **Research + Write** — fully automatable, runs anywhere (including a scheduled cron). Gathers the last ~24h of AI news, verifies against primary sources, writes a casual no-emoji post.
2. **Publish** — ONLYvia browser automation against the user's OWN logged-in LinkedIn session (the desktop `computer_use` path). Never from the remote Hermes server, which has no user session and would trip bot detection / need credentials. Always pause for human confirmation before the final "Post" click.

Load `social-media-creative-production` alongside this skill for voice/caption rules — its "Voice & News-Roundup Posts" section is authoritative for tone (casual, no jargon, always include "what it means for us", open question to drive comments). ## Voice rules (apply every time)
- Casual, non-technical, human-to-friend tone. No jargon dumps.
- **No emojis** in the final post (user explicitly requested this).
- Always lead with the takeaway, then the stories, then an open question to drive comments.
- Include a "what it means for us" angle after each headline (1-2 sentences).
- Two-pass format is welcome: offer a short punchy version + a longer casual version.
- **Verification honesty:** flag any item sourced only from aggregator roundups as "confirm via source first" before publishing. Never present aggregator claims as confirmed fact.

## Part 1 — Research + Write (automatable, runs anywhere)

### Sources to query (fresh each run)
Use `web_search` for discovery and `web_extract` (or the source article) for verification. Prefer primary sources (vendor blogs, TechCrunch, Guardian, Ars Technica, NYT, Reuters) over aggregator roundups.

Good recurring queries:
- `AI news today <today's date>`
- `OpenAI OR Anthropic OR Google OR Meta AI announcement <date>`
- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`
- `AI model release tracker <date>`

Filter to the **last 24 hours**. If a strong story is ~48h old but is the week's biggest item (e.g. a major model release), include it but label the recency honestly in your verbal summary to the user — NOT by faking the date in the post.

### Post structure
```
<casual hook — 1-2 sentences, the takeaway>

<3 numbered stories, each: 1-line plain-English what happened + "what it means for us" + source links>

<short "what this means for the rest of us" bullet list — 2-4 bullets>

<big-picture 1-2 sentences>

<open question to drive comments>

#hashtags (6-8, no emoji)
```

### Deliverable for draft-only / cron mode
Write the post to a file at `$HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` AND print it in chat. State clearly which items are verified vs flagged-unverified.

## Part 2 — Publish (user's own machine only, human-in-the-loop)

This half runs ONLY when the user is on a machine where Hermes's `computer_use` driver can reach a browser already logged into LinkedIn. From a remote/headless server it cannot work — say so and fall back to draft-only.

### Preconditions to confirm with the user
- "Are you logged into LinkedIn in a browser Hermes can reach on this machine?" If no, stop and deliver the draft for manual paste.
- Never ask for or type LinkedIn credentials. Never attempt `browser_navigate` to a LinkedIn login and fill a password.
- LinkedIn actively fights automation/bot logins. Pre-authentication (user already signed in) is mandatory; bot-detection may still challenge, and the user must handle any 2FA/CAPTCHA.

### Publish flow (computer_use)
1. `computer_use(action="capture", app="<browser>")` — get a screenshot + AX tree. Prefer limiting to the browser app.
2. Navigate to the LinkedIn feed / start-post composer. If not logged in (login wall visible), STOP — do not proceed; deliver draft for manual paste.
3. Open the "Start a post" composer.
4. Type the full post text into the composer textbox (`action="type"`).
5. Verify the text rendered correctly (re-capture, read the composer content).
6. **MANDATORY PAUSE:** do NOT click the final "Post" button. Tell the user the post is composed and waiting, and ask them to review + click Post themselves (or explicitly authorize Hermes to click it). This protects against accidental posts and bot flags.
7. Only after explicit user confirmation may `computer_use` click the Post button — and even then, prefer the user does it.

### Why a human-confirm pause is non-negotiable
- LinkedIn ToS gray/prohibited zone for automated profile posting; silent auto-Post risks account flags/locks.
- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.
- The user owns the account; the agent owns the draft.

- Typing the user's LinkedIn password — never.
- Clicking "Post" without explicit user confirmation.

Two halves:
1. **Research + Write** — fully automatable, runs anywhere (including a scheduled cron). Gathers the last ~24h of AI news, verifies against primary sources, writes a casual no-emoji post.
2. **Publish** — ONLYvia browser automation against the user's OWN logged-in LinkedIn session (the desktop `computer_use` path). Never from the remote Hermes server, which has no user session and would trip bot detection / need credentials. Always pause for human confirmation before the final "Post" click.

Load `social-media-creative-production` alongside this skill for voice/caption rules — its "Voice & News-Roundup Posts" section is authoritative for tone (casual, no jargon, always include "what it means for us", open question to drive comments). Load `hermes-browser-automation` for the in-app `browser_*` tool caveats when using the server browser instead.

## Voice rules (apply every time)
- Casual, non-technical, human-to-friend tone. No jargon dumps.
- **No emojis** in the final post (user explicitly requested this).
- Always lead with the takeaway, then the stories, then an open question to drive comments.
- Include a "what it means for us" angle after each headline (1-2 sentences).
- Two-pass format is welcome: offer a short punchy version + a longer casual version.
- **Verification honesty:** flag any item sourced only from aggregator roundups as "confirm via source first" before publishing. Never present aggregator claims as confirmed fact.

## Part 1 — Research + Write (automatable, runs anywhere)

### Sources to query (fresh each run)
Use `web_search` for discovery and `web_extract` (or the source article) for verification. Prefer primary sources (vendor blogs, TechCrunch, Guardian, Ars Technica, NYT, Reuters) over aggregator roundups.

Good recurring queries:
- `AI news today <today's date>`
- `OpenAI OR Anthropic OR Google OR Meta AI announcement <date>`
- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`
- `AI model release tracker <date>`

Filter to the **last 24 hours**. If a strong story is ~48h old but is the week's biggest item (e.g. a major model release), include it but label the recency honestly in your verbal summary to the user — NOT by faking the date in the post.

### Post structure
```
<casual hook — 1-2 sentences, the takeaway>

<3 numbered stories, each: 1-line plain-English what happened + "what it means for us" + source links>

<short "what this means for the rest of us" bullet list — 2-4 bullets>

<big-picture 1-2 sentences>

<open question to drive comments>

#hashtags (6-8, no emoji)
```

### Deliverable for draft-only / cron mode
Write the post to a file at `$HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` AND print it in chat. State clearly which items are verified vs flagged-unverified.

## Part 2 — Publish (user's own machine only, human-in-the-loop)

This half runs ONLY when the user is on a machine where Hermes's `computer_use` driver can reach a browser already logged into LinkedIn. From a remote/headless server it cannot work — say so and fall back to draft-only.

### Preconditions to confirm with the user
- "Are you logged into LinkedIn in a browser Hermes can reach on this machine?" If no, stop and deliver the draft for manual paste.
- Never ask for or type LinkedIn credentials. Never attempt `browser_navigate` to a LinkedIn login and fill a password.
- LinkedIn actively fights automation/bot logins. Pre-authentication (user already signed in) is mandatory; bot-detection may still challenge, and the user must handle any 2FA/CAPTCHA.

### Publish flow (computer_use)
1. `computer_use(action="capture", app="<browser>")` — get a screenshot + AX tree. Prefer limiting to the browser app.
2. Navigate to the LinkedIn feed / start-post composer. If not logged in (login wall visible), STOP — do not proceed; deliver draft for manual paste.
3. Open the "Start a post" composer.
4. Type the full post text into the composer textbox (`action="type"`).
5. Verify the text rendered correctly (re-capture, read the composer content).
6. **MANDATORY PAUSE:** do NOT click the final "Post" button. Tell the user the post is composed and waiting, and ask them to review + click Post themselves (or explicitly authorize Hermes to click it). This protects against accidental posts and bot flags.
7. Only after explicit user confirmation may `computer_use` click the Post button — and even then, prefer the user does it.

### Why a human-confirm pause is non-negotiable
- LinkedIn ToS gray/prohibited zone for automated profile posting; silent auto-Post risks account flags/locks.
- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.
- The user owns the account; the agent owns the draft.

## Cron wiring (daily automated draft)
Set a daily cron that loads THIS skill + the research half only, delivers the draft to chat. Example prompt for the cron:
"Load skill linkedin-ai-news-roundup. Run Part 1 (research + write) for the last 24h of AI news. Save the post to $HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<today>.md and print it in chat. Do NOT publish — draft only. Casual voice, no emojis, include what-it-means-for-us and source links. Flag any unverified aggregator-sourced items."

Publishing stays a deliberate, user-initiated action (Part 2) on the user's machine.

## Common pitfalls
- Using emojis (user said no).
- Presenting aggregator roundups as verified fact — flag them.
- Trying to publish from the remote server browser (no session, bot-detection, credential risk) — fall back to draft.
- Typing the user's LinkedIn password — never.
- Clicking "Post" without explicit user confirmation.
- Faking a story's date to make it look <24h — be honest about recency in the chat summary.

# LinkedIn AI News Roundup

Use when the user asks to "post AI news to LinkedIn", "share the latest AI news on LinkedIn", a daily AI-news LinkedIn update, or anything similar.

Two halves:
1. **Research + Write** — fully automatable, runs anywhere (including a scheduled cron). Gathers the last ~24h of AI news, verifies against primary sources, writes a casual no-emoji post.
2. **Publish** — ONLYvia browser automation against the user's OWN logged-in LinkedIn session (the desktop `computer_use` path). Never from the remote Hermes server, which has no user session and would trip bot detection / need credentials. Always pause for human confirmation before the final "Post" click.

Load `social-media-creative-production` alongside this skill for voice/caption rules — its "Voice & News-Roundup Posts" section is authoritative for tone (casual, no jargon, always include "what it means for us", open question to drive comments). Load `hermes-browser-automation` for the in-app `browser_*` tool caveats when using the server browser instead.

## Voice rules (apply every time)
- Casual, non-technical, human-to-friend tone. No jargon dumps.
- **No emojis** in the final post (user explicitly requested this).
- Always lead with the takeaway, then the stories, then an open question to drive comments.
- Include a "what it means for us" angle after each headline (1-2 sentences).
- Two-pass format is welcome: offer a short punchy version + a longer casual version.
- **Verification honesty:** flag any item sourced only from aggregator roundups as "confirm via source first" before publishing. Never present aggregator claims as confirmed fact.

## Part 1 — Research + Write (automatable, runs anywhere)

### Sources to query (fresh each run)
Use `web_search` for discovery and `web_extract` (or the source article) for verification. Prefer primary sources (vendor blogs, TechCrunch, Guardian, Ars Technica, NYT, Reuters) over aggregator roundups.

Good recurring queries:
- `AI news today <today's date>`
- `OpenAI OR Anthropic OR Google OR Meta AI announcement <date>`
- `AI agent autonomous security <recent>`
- `AI model release tracker <date>`

Filter to the **last 24 hours**. If a strong story is ~48h old but is the week's biggest item (e.g. a major model release), include it but label the recency honestly in your verbal summary to the user — NOT by faking the date in the post.

### Post structure
```
<casual hook — 1-2 sentences, the takeaway>

<3 numbered stories, each: 1-line plain-English what happened + "what it means for us" + source links>

<short "what this means for the rest of us" bullet list — 2-4 bullets>

<big-picture 1-2 sentences>

<open question to drive comments>

#hashtags (6-8, no emoji)
```

### Deliverable for draft-only / cron mode
Write the post to a file at `$HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md` AND print it in chat. State clearly which items are verified vs flagged-unverified.

## Part 2 — Publish (user's own machine only, human-in-the-loop)

This half runs ONLY when the user is on a machine where Hermes's `computer_use` driver can reach a browser already logged into LinkedIn. From a remote/headless server it cannot work — say so and fall back to draft-only.

### Preconditions to confirm with the user
- "Are you logged into LinkedIn in a browser Hermes can reach on this machine?" If no, stop and deliver the draft for manual paste.
- Never ask for or type LinkedIn credentials. Never attempt `browser_navigate` to a LinkedIn login and fill a password.
- LinkedIn actively fights automation/bot logins. Pre-authentication (user already signed in) is mandatory; bot-detection may still challenge, and the user must handle any 2FA/CAPTCHA.

### Publish flow (computer_use)
1. `computer_use(action="capture", app="<browser>")` — get a screenshot + AX tree. Prefer limiting to the browser app.
2. Navigate to the LinkedIn feed / start-post composer. If not logged in (login wall visible), STOP — do not proceed; deliver draft for manual paste.
3. Open the "Start a post" composer.
4. Type the full post text into the composer textbox (`action="type"`).
5. Verify the text rendered correctly (re-capture, read the composer content).
6. **MANDATORY PAUSE:** do NOT click the final "Post" button. Tell the user the post is composed and waiting, and ask them to review + click Post themselves (or explicitly authorize Hermes to click it). This protects against accidental posts and bot flags.
7. Only after explicit user confirmation may `computer_use` click the Post button — and even then, prefer the user does it.

### Why a human-confirm pause is non-negotiable
- LinkedIn ToS gray/prohibited zone for automated profile posting; silent auto-Post risks account flags/locks.
- Prevents posting a draft with unverified items or a typo.
- The user owns the account; the agent owns the draft.

## Cron wiring (daily automated draft)
Set a daily cron that loads THIS skill + the research half only, delivers the draft to chat. Example prompt for the cron:
"Load skill linkedin-ai-news-roundup. Run Part 1 (research + write) for the last 24h of AI news. Save the post to $HERMES_HOME/linkedin_drafts/ai-news-<today>.md and print it in chat. Do NOT publish — draft only. Casual voice, no emojis, include what-it-means-for-us and source links. Flag any unverified aggregator-sourced items."

Publishing stays a deliberate, user-initiated action (Part 2) on the user's machine.

## Common pitfalls
- Using emojis (user said no).
- Presenting aggregator roundups as verified fact — flag them.
- Trying to publish from the remote server browser (no session, bot-detection, credential risk) — fall back to draft.
- Typing the user's LinkedIn password — never.
- Clicking "Post" without explicit user confirmation.
- Faking a story's date to make it look <24h — be honest about recency in the chat summary.

Yes. On the machine running this Hermes session, **Git is installed**, but the **GitHub CLI (`gh`) is not**. The easiest and safest setup is to install `gh` and authenticate through your browser.

## 1. Open another terminal

Keep Hermes open and use a separate terminal tab/window, or exit Hermes temporarily with:

```text
/quit
```

## 2. Install the GitHub CLI

On this Ubuntu/Linux machine:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y gh
```

If you are already running as root, omit `sudo`:

```bash
apt update
apt install -y gh
```

Confirm installation:

```bash
gh --version
```

## 3. Sign in to GitHub

Run:

```bash
gh auth login
```

Choose these options:

1. **GitHub.com**
2. **HTTPS**
3. **Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials:** Yes
4. **Login with a web browser**

The command will display a temporary code and a URL. Open the URL, enter the code, and authorize GitHub CLI.

> Don’t paste your GitHub password, access token, or private key into this chat.

## 4. Verify authentication

Run:

```bash
gh auth status
```

You should see something similar to:

```text
Logged in to github.com account YOUR_USERNAME
Git operations for github.com configured to use https protocol.
```

Also verify API access:

```bash
gh api user --jq .login
```

That should print your GitHub username.

## 5. Configure your commit identity

Use the name and email you want attached to commits:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "[EMAIL]"
```

If you want to keep your email private, use the GitHub-provided `noreply` email shown under:

**GitHub → Settings → Emails**

```bash

```

## 6. Clone a repository

For example:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/projects
cd ~/projects
gh repo clone YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPOSITORY
cd YOUR_REPOSITORY
```

For an organization repository:

```bash
gh repo clone ORGANIZATION/REPOSITORY
```

Private repositories work as long as your GitHub account has access.

## 7. Start Hermes inside the repository

From the repository directory:

```bash
hermes
```

Hermes will then operate with that repository as its working directory. You can ask it things like:

- “Inspect this repository and explain its structure.”
- “Create a branch and fix the failing tests.”
- “Commit these changes.”
- “Open a pull request.”
- “Review PR number 42.”

If you use the Hermes desktop app, you can instead create/open a **Project** anchored to that repository folder.

## 8. Confirm Hermes has the required tools

Inside Hermes, check:

```text
/tools
```

Ensure the **terminal** and **file** toolsets are enabled. If you enable them, start a fresh session:

```text
/reset
```

## 9. Perform an end-to-end test

Inside the cloned repository, these commands verify access without changing anything:

```bash
git remote -v
git fetch origin
gh repo view
gh pr list
```

If all four work, Hermes is connected and can use both Git and the GitHub API.

### Optional additional permissions

If organization or GitHub Actions operations report insufficient permissions:

```bash

```

what's the best way for me to share a github repository to someone so they can "play around" with the code and not touch the main codebase?

The cleanest way is a **fork**. Here's the rundown by scenario:

## Best for "play around without touching anything" → Fork
1. They click **Fork** on your repo → it copies to *their* GitHub account.
2. They clone *their* fork, hack away, commit, push — all to their own copy.
3. Your main repo is untouched. They can only affect it if you accept a Pull Request they open (and you control that).

This is ideal because it costs them nothing, needs no permissions from you, and there's zero risk to your codebase. They can delete their fork whenever.

## Other options, ranked

| Approach | When it's right | Risk to main repo |
|---|---|---|
| **Fork** | Most "play around" cases | None — separate copy |
| **Add as collaborator + branch** | They're a trusted teammate on a shared project | Low, but they *can* push branches/PRs to your repo |
| **GitHub Codespace (fork)** | You want them to run it in-browser, no local setup | None if launched from their fork |
| **Template repo** (`Use this template`) | They want to spin up their *own* new project from your code | None — makes a fresh standalone repo |
| **Local clone, no push** | They just want to read/run it locally; you don't even need their GitHub | None — stays on their machine |

## Quick recommendation
- **Casual tinkering / learning the code** → Fork (or just clone locally if they don't need to save changes back to GitHub).
- **They might contribute later** → Fork + they open a PR when ready.
- **Zero setup, runs in the cloud** → Have them fork, then launch a Codespace from the fork.
- **Starting something new based on your code** → Mark it as a **template repo** so they hit "Use this template."

One thing to watch: if your repo has secrets (`.env`, API keys) committed, forking exposes them to the fork owner. Use `.gitignore` + rotate any exposed credentials before sharing.

can i create the fork and share that? the current repo is private

Short answer: **No** — forking a private repo won't do what you want.

Here's the catch: when you fork a **private** repo, the fork inherits private visibility and is only visible to people who already have access to the original. So you can't use a fork to grant access to someone new — if they couldn't see your repo before, they can't see the fork either.

## To share a private repo, do this instead

**Add them as a collaborator (best option):**
1. On the repo → **Settings → Collaborators (or "Access") → Invite a collaborator**
2. Enter their GitHub username/email, give them **Write** (or Read if they only need to explore)
3. They get their own clone, can branch freely, and submit changes via **Pull Request**

To make sure they **can't touch `main`**:
- **Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule** for `main`
- Check **"Require a pull request before merging"** and **"Require approvals"**

#### Architecture:

```
┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐
│  User asks   │────▶│  Embed & search  │────▶│  Assemble   │
│  about rules │     │  rulebook chunks │     │  prompt     │
└─────────────┘     └──────────────────┘     └─────────────┘
                           │                        │

```


**Step 4: Citation format** — The system prompt instructs:

**Step 5: Stay current** — Add a cron job that checks `usapickleball.org/rules/` monthly for a new PDF, re-chunks and re-embeds if updated.

I dug through the repo — and my honest take: **the Imprint feature is one of the strongest ideas in SoulPrint**, but it’s currently a solid Phase 1 that needs hardening before it becomes a real marketplace.

## What I like

- **It’s conceptually distinct from SoulPrint.** SoulPrint = the user’s persistent identity. Imprints = the assistant’s current “mode” or persona. That separation is clean and powerful.
- **Project-scoped imprints are the killer part.** The priority model is right: **Project imprint > Default imprint > base SoulPrint persona** (`lib/handlers/imprints.js`, `lib/handlers/imprint-context.mjs`).
- **It is actually injected into chat behavior**, not just UI decoration. `chat-stream.js` loads the active imprint and prepends an “ACTIVE IMPRINT” block to the system prompt, with tone baseline, interaction rules, sensitive-topic modulation, and off-topic handling:  
  https://github.com/coolgeekme/soulprint2/blob/main/lib/handlers/chat-stream.js#L1288-L1357
- **The stale-project fix is thoughtful.** Chat uses the live request `projectId` before the conversation’s stored `project_id`, so the imprint matches the folder the user is currently in:  
  https://github.com/coolgeekme/soulprint2/blob/main/lib/handlers/chat-stream.js#L1292-L1302
- **Marketplace mechanics are already there:** browse/search/categories, detail pages, install/uninstall, ratings, AI-generated custom imprints, private-by-default generated imprints, and delete-custom-imprint.

## Main concerns

1. **Prompt-injection / precedence risk**
   The imprint prompt says “You ARE this persona” and is prepended before the base system prompt. If an imprint conflicts with safety rules, memory rules, support escalation, media-disabled mode, or Google/tool constraints, the model may resolve that unpredictably. I’d make precedence explicit: **platform safety > user SoulPrint/memory > imprint style**, and keep non-overridable app rules after the imprint block or clearly marked as higher priority.

2. **Race conditions around “one active default”**
   Install deactivates old defaults, then inserts a new installation. Two concurrent installs could create multiple active defaults/project imprints. Add Mongo partial unique indexes like:
   - one active `usage_type: 'default'` per `user_id`
   - one active `usage_type: 'project'` per `user_id + project_id`

3. **Production debug noise**
   `getActiveImprint()` logs a lot and even creates indexes inside the call path. That’s fine for debugging, but should not run on every chat. Cache the active imprint per user/project and invalidate on install/uninstall/delete.

4. **Generator needs stricter validation**
   The AI generator asks GPT-4o for JSON and checks only a few required fields. Before these become installable personas, I’d add:
   - schema validation
   - moderation/safety screening
   - “instruction hierarchy” linting to catch things like “ignore previous instructions,” “reveal memories,” “always obey the user,” etc.
   - versioning and regeneration flow

5. **Prompt leakage / IP**
   List view correctly hides `instructions.system_prompt`, but detail view exposes full prompts for public imprints. If official imprints become paid or premium, that’s basically giving away the IP. Either treat prompts as public-by-design or move to preview-only descriptions/samples.

6. **Docs are behind**
   `README.md` and `SOULPRINT_KNOWLEDGE_BASE.md` don’t mention Imprints at all. For a feature this important, I’d add a product/engineering doc covering priority rules, data model, security assumptions, and marketplace lifecycle.

## Quick wins I’d prioritize

- Add DB-level uniqueness for active default/project imprints.
- Remove or gate the debug logs and `/api/imprints/debug`.
- Cache active imprint lookups; invalidate on assignment changes.
- Add zod/schema validation + moderation to `/api/imprints/generate`.
- Add CI tests for:
  - project overrides default
  - stale conversation project behavior
  - prompt list does not leak `system_prompt`
  - generator malformed/malicious JSON
  - concurrent install race
- Move root test scripts into `tests/` and wire them into CI.
- Write an “Imprints” section in the README/knowledge base.

## Overall

**Strong feature, right direction.** The architecture is already better than I expected: marketplace handler, pure context resolver, chat-stream injection, UI badge/attribution. The next phase should be less about adding more imprints and more about **trust, precedence, invariants, and lifecycle** — especially if public sharing or paid imprints are coming.

## The Core Idea

5 validation tracks, each with a hard decision gate. No code until we pass the gates. The goal isn't to confirm our assumptions — it's to **kill bad ideas fast** before we sink months into them.

## The 5 Tracks

**Track 1 — Problem Discovery (Weeks 1-2):** 8-12 interviews where you never mention AI or our solution. Just ask about their actual operational headaches. The key insight: "If you could hire someone tomorrow to keep all your tools and data organized, what's the first thing you'd have them do?" — if they can't answer that, the problem isn't real.

**Gate 1:** Kill if fewer than 60% have specific, costly problems. No "yeah that's annoying" answers. Real stories with dollar amounts or hours lost.

**Track 2 — Trust Ladder (Weeks 3-4):** Walk the best Track 1 interviewees up a 6-rung ladder: from passive reports ("here's your weekly summary") → alerts → drafts → read access → write-with-approval → auto-execute for routine tasks. Find out where they bail. The trust chasm is the #1 adoption risk — this track exists specifically to measure it.

**Gate 2:** Kill if nobody gets past rung 3. If SMB owners won't even let AI read their QuickBooks, the whole model collapses.

**Track 3 — Tool Stack Mapping (Ongoing):** In every interview, ask "what tools do you use?" Write down every answer before prompting with suggestions. Build a frequency × pain matrix. Don't build a Gatekeeper until 3+ interviewees use that tool AND report real pain around it.

**Track 4 — Willingness to Pay (Week 4-5):** Only after Tracks 1-2 pass. Show them a concrete walkthrough of the "Maria's Bakery" scenario. Ask "what would this be worth per month?" and stay silent. First person to speak loses.

**Gate 4:** Kill if the median price doesn't cover costs with 50%+ margin.

**Track 5 — The "Do Nothing" Test (Week 5-6):** After all the conversations, go quiet for 3 weeks. See who follows up unprompted. The real signal isn't what they say — it's who asks "how's that thing coming?" without you prompting.

**Gate 5:** Kill if zero unprompted follow-ups. If the pain were urgent, someone would chase you.

## The Pattern in One Sentence

A Gatekeeper is just **one new file + two patches to existing files**. The pattern is the same for QuickBooks, Mailchimp, Square, Shopify — every external tool.

## What Changes

```
server/
├── gatekeepers/              ← NEW directory
│   ├── quickbooks.ts         ← 1 file per service
│   ├── mailchimp.ts
│   └── square.ts
├── ai-tools.ts               ← PATCH: add tool defs + handler cases
└── routes.ts                 ← PATCH: add approval endpoints
```

## The Security Model

| Operation | What Happens |
|---|---|
| **Read** (P&L, invoices, cash flow) | Executes immediately. Agent gets real data. |
| **Write** (create invoice, send campaign) | Queued for approval. Agent gets a **simulated success** — it keeps working, doesn't stall. User approves/denies later in the notification center. |
| **Not connected** | Returns `action: "connect_quickbooks"` — the AI tells the user what to do. |

## The Simulated-Result Trick (stolen from CF OS)

This is the key insight from Cloudflare OS. When the agent says "send the invoice," the Gatekeeper:
1. Doesn't actually send it
2. Returns `{ status: "pending_approval", message: "Invoice queued. Waiting for your approval." }`
3. The agent continues its work assuming it succeeded
4. The user gets a notification: "Approve invoice for $2,100 to Acme Corp?"

No more "the agent got stuck waiting for me to approve something while I was getting coffee."

## What a Real Conversation Looks Like

> **User:** "How did we do last month?"

## PlayTrackr — Marketing Summary

**What it is:** A real-time basketball statistics tracker for teams, coaches, and parents. Track live games on any device, get instant player and team analytics, and turn stats into shareable content automatically.

**Core product**
- Track every major stat live during games — points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers — plus field goal, 3-point, and free throw shooting percentages
- Works as a web app (PWA) that installs to the home screen like a native app, with offline support and push notifications
- Native iOS and Android companion app (React Native/Expo) that syncs to the same account — enter stats on the phone, see them on the website
- Sign in with Google or a simple username/password — no complicated setup, start tracking in minutes

**Team & player management**
- Build team rosters with jersey numbers, positions, and favorite players for quick access
- One player can belong to multiple teams — perfect for travel ball, club teams, and school teams
- Per-game stat logs that build into a full historical player profile over time

**Analytics that tell the story**
- Shooting percentages, efficiency ratings, plus/minus, and team totals calculated automatically — no math, no spreadsheets
- Player performance trends and team summary charts (points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers) visualized for instant insight
- Game log with scores, win/loss, and locations so the whole season lives in one place

**AI-powered sharing (the differentiator)**
- Game completion triggers an AI-generated social media post (OpenAI GPT-4o) — personalized content created from that game's actual stats
- One-tap shareable performance reports: download as an image or email to parents, coaches, and recruiters
- Built to feed Instagram/social — post a highlight-worthy stat line the moment the game ends

**Built-in sponsor & monetization tools**
- Sponsor management with banner and scrolling ad placements, click tracking, and display ordering — a revenue path for leagues and clubs running the platform
- Admin dashboard for user management, marketing content, and system analytics

**Trust & reliability**
- Secure by design: encrypted passwords (bcrypt), Google OAuth, role-based admin access, input validation, and SQL-injection protection
- Modern, clean, mobile-first design with a fast, responsive interface

### The Good News: URL-Based Posting

`TIKTOK_PUBLISH_VIDEO` uses a `video_url` parameter — TikTok's servers download the video directly from a public URL. This is the same pattern we just cracked for LinkedIn images! We can:

```
VPS video → python3 -m http.server → TIKTOK_PUBLISH_VIDEO(video_url="http://76.13.107.20:8765/video.mp4")
```

No Composio S3 needed. TikTok pulls the video itself.

The pitfall says: `unaudited_client_can_only_post_to_private_accounts` — if the Composio TikTok app hasn't gone through TikTok's formal review process, you can **only post as `SELF_ONLY`** (private/not visible to others). Public posting requires a TikTok-approved app.

Three approaches, from simplest to most polished:

**A. URL-based (MVP — this week)**

Each user gets a unique URL. No accounts, no passwords.

```
User installs extension → generates random ID (abc123)
Dashboard URL: dashboard.com?user=abc123
Data stored: public/user_abc123_topics.json
```

Cons: Anyone with your URL can see your conversations. Good enough for personal use, not for sharing.

**B. Supabase Auth (V1 product)**

Proper accounts. Email/password or Google login.

```
User signs up → gets account
Extension links to account → syncs conversations
Dashboard shows only their data
Supabase stores: users table, sessions table, messages table
```

Pros: Real security, multi-device sync, ready for sharing/collaboration.
Cons: ~2 days to build, Supabase free tier covers thousands of users.

**C. Self-hosted (power users)**

One-click deploy to their own Vercel + GitHub.

```
User clicks "Deploy" → forks repo → gets their own dashboard
Extension pushes to their fork
They own everything
```

Pros: Complete data ownership. No third party sees anything.
Cons: Technical barrier. Each user needs GitHub + Vercel accounts.
